claim: MeCP2 is the defective gene in Rett syndrome and encodes a ubiquitously expressed X-linked transcription factor.
source: Rett syndrome has remained the subject of great interest since the defective gene was first identified as encoding the ubiquitously expressed X - linked transcription factor, Methyl CpG Binding Protein 2, MeCP2 (Amir et al., 1999).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Amir et al., 1999, which is the original identification of the gene.

claim: Affected males with Rett syndrome have a severe brain disorder and usually die prior to the age of two.
source: Affected males have a severe brain disorder and usually die prior to the age of two.
evidence: This is a statement about clinical characteristics of Rett syndrome in males, drawing from established medical knowledge.

claim: Affected females with Rett syndrome are mosaic due to X chromosome inactivation and live on average to ~40 years of age.
source: Affected females are mosaic due to dosage compensation by X chromosome inactivation and live on average to ~40 years of age.
evidence: This statement describes clinical characteristics of Rett syndrome in females based on established medical knowledge.

claim: Rett syndrome in females is characterized by regression of early developmental milestones, such as speech and purposeful hand motions, followed by acquisition of multiple motor abnormalities, anxiety and seizures.
source: The disease in females is characterized by regression of early developmental milestones, such as speech and purposeful hand motions, followed by the acquisition of multiple motor abnormalities, anxiety and seizures (Chahrour and Zoghbi, 2007).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Chahrour and Zoghbi, 2007.

claim: Expression of Mecp2 from the neuronal tau locus in mice prevented the appearance of some RTT-like phenotypes.
source: For example, expression of Mecp2 from the neuronal tau locus in mice prevented the appearance of some RTT-like phenotypes (Luikenhuis et al., 2004).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Luikenhuis et al., 2004.

claim: Loss and restoration of MeCP2 just in inhibitory neurons affects RTT phenotypes.
source: More recently, loss and restoration of MeCP2 just in inhibitory (Ure et al., 2016) or excitatory neurons (Meng et al., 2016) was shown to affect RTT phenotypes differentially.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Ure et al., 2016.

claim: Loss and restoration of MeCP2 just in excitatory neurons affects RTT phenotypes.
source: More recently, loss and restoration of MeCP2 just in inhibitory (Ure et al., 2016) or excitatory neurons (Meng et al., 2016) was shown to affect RTT phenotypes differentially.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Meng et al., 2016.

claim: Early immunohistochemical studies indicated that astrocytes did not express MeCP2.
source: Finally, early immunohistochemical studies indicated that astrocytes did not express MeCP2 (Akbarian et al., 2001; Shahbazian et al., 2002; Kishi and Macklis, 2004; Jung et al., 2003).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to multiple studies: Akbarian et al., 2001; Shahbazian et al., 2002; Kishi and Macklis, 2004; Jung et al., 2003.

claim: Astrocytes express MeCP2.
source: Thus, it was very unexpected when it was first reported that astrocytes express MeCP2 (Ballas et al., 2009) and that restoration of MeCP2 expression specifically in astrocytes, in otherwise null mice, delayed the progression of RTT- like symptoms (Lioy et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Ballas et al., 2009.

claim: Restoration of MeCP2 expression specifically in astrocytes, in otherwise null mice, delayed the progression of RTT-like symptoms.
source: Thus, it was very unexpected when it was first reported that astrocytes express MeCP2 (Ballas et al., 2009) and that restoration of MeCP2 expression specifically in astrocytes, in otherwise null mice, delayed the progression of RTT- like symptoms (Lioy et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Lioy et al., 2011.

claim: Astrocyte stimulation in wild-type mice increases excitatory synaptic activity.
source: We find that astrocyte stimulation in wild-type mice increases excitatory synaptic activity that is absent in male mice lacking MeCP2 globally.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript, including dual patch clamp recordings showing increased synaptic event frequency following astrocyte stimulation.

claim: Astrocyte-mediated increase in excitatory synaptic activity is absent in male mice lacking MeCP2 globally.
source: We find that astrocyte stimulation in wild-type mice increases excitatory synaptic activity that is absent in male mice lacking MeCP2 globally.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript showing no increase in synaptic event frequency in MeCP2 null mice following astrocyte stimulation.

claim: The defect in astrocyte-mediated neuronal signaling is dependent upon MeCP2 expression status in the astrocytes and not in the neurons.
source: We find that the defect is dependent upon MeCP2 expression status in the astrocytes and not in the neurons.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from mosaic female mice showing that MeCP2-positive astrocytes can activate MeCP2-negative neurons, but MeCP2-negative astrocytes cannot activate MeCP2-positive neurons.

claim: Neurons held at −80 mV are associated consistently with spontaneous synaptic events that are all inwardly directed.
source: Neuronal recordings were associated consistently with spontaneous synaptic events that were all inwardly directed (Figure 2a).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2a.

claim: The spontaneous synaptic events in neurons ranged in frequency from 99 ± 39 events/m to 537 ± 147 events/m.
source: The spontaneous synaptic events ranged in frequency from 99 ± 39 events/m to 537 ± 147 events/m and a corresponding amplitude range of 4.6 ± 2 pA to 363 ± 122 pA for the smallest and largest events in each recording.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental measurements from neuronal recordings.

claim: The spontaneous synaptic events in neurons had a corresponding amplitude range of 4.6 ± 2 pA to 363 ± 122 pA for the smallest and largest events in each recording.
source: The spontaneous synaptic events ranged in frequency from 99 ± 39 events/m to 537 ± 147 events/m and a corresponding amplitude range of 4.6 ± 2 pA to 363 ± 122 pA for the smallest and largest events in each recording.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental measurements from neuronal recordings.

claim: All astrocytes were quiescent, including during the time periods directly following depolarization.
source: By contrast, all astrocytes were quiescent, including during the time periods directly following the depolarization that was used to activate synaptic responses in the proximal neuron.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental observations from astrocyte recordings.

claim: Depolarization of astrocytes using 20 consecutive 10 ms voltage steps from −80 mV to +60 mV led to an increase in the frequency of synaptic currents in the proximal, paired neuron.
source: Depolarization of the astrocytes using 20 consecutive 10 ms voltage steps from −80 mV to +60 mV led to an increase in the frequency of the synaptic currents in the proximal, paired neuron (Figure 2a–b).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 2a-b.

claim: The increase in event frequency following astrocyte depolarization occurred within the first 5 s following the onset of astrocyte depolarization, with the peak increase occurring within 40 s.
source: The increase in event frequency occurred within the first 5 s following the onset of astrocyte depolarization, with the peak increase occurring within 40 s as indicated by the color-coded asterisks (Figure 2b).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2b.

claim: Astrocyte depolarization resulted in a significant increase in the frequency of synaptic currents (pre-stim: 272 ± 180 events/m, post-stim: 337 ± 143 events/m, p=0.002, n = 14).
source: Cumulative data from neuronal recordings indicated a significant increase in the frequency of synaptic currents following astrocyte depolarization (pre-stim: 272 ± 180 events/m, post-stim: 337 ± 143 events/m, p=0.002, n = 14) (Figure 2c)
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data with statistical analysis shown in Figure 2c.

claim: Astrocyte depolarization resulted in an average 1.48 ± 0.58 fold increase in synaptic event frequency.
source: which corresponded to an average 1.48 ± 0.58 fold increase in frequency (Figure 2d).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2d.

claim: There was no overall difference in the average amplitude of synaptic events before and after astrocyte depolarization (pre-stim: 31 ± 24 pA, post-stim: 30 ± 27 pA; 1.02 ± 0.28 fold change).
source: when expressed as fold-change for individual experiments, there was no overall difference in the average amplitude before and after stimulation (pre-stim: 31 ± 24 pA, post-stim: 30 ± 27 pA; 1.02 ± 0.28 fold change; Figure 2f).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2f.

claim: Par1 is expressed in astrocytes at both the mRNA and protein levels.
source: Par1 is expressed in astrocytes at both the mRNA (http://astrocyternaseq.org/addgene?query=F2r), and protein levels (Junge et al., 2004).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Junge et al., 2004 and reference to an online database.

claim: Immuno-labeling of barrel cortex with a Par1 antibody resulted in fluorescence that was associated exclusively with GFAP-positive astrocytes, with no measurable labeling in wild-type NeuN-positive neurons.
source: In our hands, immuno-labeling of barrel cortex with a Par1 antibody resulted in fluorescence that was associated exclusively with GFAP-positive astrocytes, with no measurable labeling in wild-type NeuN-positive neurons (Figure 3a).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 3a.

claim: Par1 is activated normally by serine proteases and by the synthetic peptide agonist, TFLLR, resulting in Gq-coupled release of intracellular calcium.
source: Par1 is activated normally by serine proteases and by the synthetic peptide agonist, TFLLR, resulting in Gq-coupled release of intracellular calcium (Hollenberg et al., 1997; Ubl and Reiser, 1997).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Hollenberg et al., 1997 and Ubl and Reiser, 1997.

claim: Application of 500 μM TFLLR to wild-type astrocytes resulted in an increase in synaptic event frequency in the proximal neuron recording.
source: Like depolarization, the application of 500 μM TFFLR (EC50 = 1.9 μM) to wild-type astrocytes consistently resulted in an increase in synaptic event frequency in the proximal neuron recording, qualitatively similar to that seen with astrocyte depolarization (Figure 4a).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4a.

claim: TFLLR application to astrocytes resulted in a significant increase in synaptic event frequency (pre-TFLLR: 169 ± 81 events/m, post-TFLLR: 254 ± 116 events/m, p=0.004, n = 10).
source: Moreover, a significant increase in synaptic event frequency was recorded for astrocyte-neuron pairs tested (pre-TFLLR: 169 ± 81 events/m, post-TFLLR: 254 ± 116 events/m, p=0.004, n = 10) (Figure 4c).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data with statistical analysis shown in Figure 4c.

claim: TFLLR application resulted in an average 1.59 ± 0.16 fold increase in synaptic event frequency.
source: When expressed as fold change, an average 1.59 ± 0.16 fold increase was observed (Figure 4d).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4d.

claim: There was no change in amplitude pre- and post-TFLLR application.
source: Again, as in the depolarization paradigm there was no change in amplitude pre- and post-TFLLR application (Figure 4e–f).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 4e-f.

claim: Application of 50 μM GABA depolarized neurons to levels sufficient for action potential generation in perforated patch recordings.
source: Recordings from 16 neurons revealed that application of 50 μM GABA depolarized the neuron to levels sufficient for action potential generation (Figure 5a).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5a.

claim: The depolarizing effect of GABA was reversibly inhibited following treatment with 20 μM gabazine.
source: The depolarizing effect of GABA in these recordings was reversibly inhibited following treatment with 20 μM gabazine (Figure 5b–c).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 5b-c.

claim: When held at 0 mV under current clamp, 50 μM GABA application led to a hyperpolarization.
source: When held at 0 mV under current clamp, 50 μM GABA application led to a hyperpolarization (Figure 5d), which was reversibly inhibited following treatment with 20 μM gabazine (Figure 5e–f), all pointing to an excitatory profile at this developmental stage (p10-12).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5d.

claim: GABA has an excitatory profile at the p10-12 developmental stage.
source: When held at 0 mV under current clamp, 50 μM GABA application led to a hyperpolarization (Figure 5d), which was reversibly inhibited following treatment with 20 μM gabazine (Figure 5e–f), all pointing to an excitatory profile at this developmental stage (p10-12).
evidence: This claim is inferred from the experimental data showing depolarization at resting potential and hyperpolarization at 0 mV, consistent with an excitatory chloride gradient.

claim: Treatment with 20 µM gabazine reduced 86% of the outward events (pre-gabazine: 18 ± 8 events/m, post-gabazine: 2.6 ± 1.3 events/m; p=0.008, n = 8).
source: Under basal conditions, 86% of the outward events were inhibited by 20 µM gabazine (pre-gabazine: 18 ± 8 events/m, post-gabazine: 2.6 ± 1.3 events/m; p=0.008, n = 8) with no significant contribution by inward currents (pre-gabazine: 101 ± 46 events/m, post-gabazine: 85 ± 35 events/m; p=0.117, n = 8) (Figure 6—figure supplement 1a).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data with statistical analysis shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1a.

claim: Inhibition of GluRs with AP5/NBQX (50 μM/ 5 μM) reduced the inward current frequency 66% (pre-AP5/NBQX: 104 ± 45 events/m, post-AP5/NBQX: 35 ± 17 events/m; p=0.0005, n = 12).
source: Inhibition of GluRs with AP5/NBQX (50 μM/ 5 μM) reduced the inward current frequency 66% (pre-AP5/NBQX: 104 ± 45 events/m, post-AP5/NBQX: 35 ± 17 events/m; p=0.0005, n = 12), with no significant contributions from the outward current class (pre-AP5/NBQX: 38 ± 13 events/m, post-AP5/NBQX events/m: 41 ± 18, p=0.386, n = 12) (Figure 6—figure supplement 1b).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data with statistical analysis shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1b.

claim: TFLLR application increased the frequency of glutamate-mediated currents by an average 1.67 ± 0.43 fold (pre-TFFLR: 147 ± 63 events/m, post-TFFLR: 236 ± 92 events/m, p=0.002, n = 10).
source: In wild-type recordings, TFFLR application increased the frequency of glutamate- mediated currents by an average 1.67 ± 0.43 fold (pre-TFFLR: 147 ± 63 events/m, post-TFFLR: 236 ± 92 events/m, p=0.002, n = 10) (Figure 6b–c).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data with statistical analysis shown in Figures 6b-c.

claim: GABA-mediated currents were increased 1.53 ± 0.46 fold in 8 out of 10 recordings (pre-TFFLR: 48 ± 23 events/m, post-TFFLR: 69 ± 34 events/m, p=0.009, n = 10).
source: GABA-mediated currents were increased 1.53 ± 0.46 fold in 8 out of 10 recordings (pre-TFFLR: 48 ± 23 events/m, post-TFFLR: 69 ± 34 events/m, p=0.009, n = 10; Figure 6d–e).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data with statistical analysis shown in Figures 6d-e.

claim: Treatment with 20 μM gabazine reduced the average basal frequency by 41% (pre: 147 ± 27 events/min post: 87 ± 31 events/min; p=0.001, n = 11).
source: Treatment with 20 μM gabazine reduced the average basal frequency by 41% (pre: 147 ± 27 events/min post: 87 ± 31 events/min; p=0.001, n = 11) and reduced the TFLLR-induced response by 59% (pre: 260 ± 120 events/min, post: 107 ± 41 events/min; p=0.004, n = 9).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data with statistical analysis.

claim: Gabazine reduced the TFLLR-induced response by 59% (pre: 260 ± 120 events/min, post: 107 ± 41 events/min; p=0.004, n = 9).
source: Treatment with 20 μM gabazine reduced the average basal frequency by 41% (pre: 147 ± 27 events/min post: 87 ± 31 events/min; p=0.001, n = 11) and reduced the TFLLR-induced response by 59% (pre: 260 ± 120 events/min, post: 107 ± 41 events/min; p=0.004, n = 9).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data with statistical analysis.

claim: Addition of a 50 μM AP5 and 5 μM NBQX cocktail led to an average 30% reduction in basal event frequency (pre: 121 ± 79 events/min, post: 85 ± 66 events/min; p=0.008, n = 8).
source: Addition of a 50 μM AP5 and 5 μM NBQX cocktail to block both AMPA and NMDA receptors led to an average 30% reduction in basal event frequency (pre: 121 ± 79 events/min, post: 85 ± 66 events/min; p=0.008, n = 8) and reduced the TFLLR-induced increase in synaptic current frequency by 44% (pre: 120 ± 58/min, post: 67 ± 47/min; p=0.0156, n = 7).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data with statistical analysis.

claim: AP5/NBQX reduced the TFLLR-induced increase in synaptic current frequency by 44% (pre: 120 ± 58/min, post: 67 ± 47/min; p=0.0156, n = 7).
source: Addition of a 50 μM AP5 and 5 μM NBQX cocktail to block both AMPA and NMDA receptors led to an average 30% reduction in basal event frequency (pre: 121 ± 79 events/min, post: 85 ± 66 events/min; p=0.008, n = 8) and reduced the TFLLR-induced increase in synaptic current frequency by 44% (pre: 120 ± 58/min, post: 67 ± 47/min; p=0.0156, n = 7).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data with statistical analysis.

claim: Treatment with TFLLR and gabazine blocked the outward currents (pre-TFFLR: 9 ± 2 events/m, post-TFFLR: 9 ± 3 events/m, p=0.732, n = 14).
source: Treatment with TFLLR and gabazine blocked the outward currents (pre-TFFLR: 9 ± 2 events/m, post-TFFLR: 9 ± 3 events/m, p=0.732, n = 14) (Figure 6f), but left untouched the increase in inward event frequency (pre-TFFLR: 169 ± 58 events/m, post-TFFLR: 195 ± 74 events/m, p=0.004, n = 14; Figure 6f).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data with statistical analysis shown in Figure 6f.

claim: Treatment with TFLLR and gabazine left untouched the increase in inward event frequency (pre-TFFLR: 169 ± 58 events/m, post-TFFLR: 195 ± 74 events/m, p=0.004, n = 14).
source: Treatment with TFLLR and gabazine blocked the outward currents (pre-TFFLR: 9 ± 2 events/m, post-TFFLR: 9 ± 3 events/m, p=0.732, n = 14) (Figure 6f), but left untouched the increase in inward event frequency (pre-TFFLR: 169 ± 58 events/m, post-TFFLR: 195 ± 74 events/m, p=0.004, n = 14; Figure 6f).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data with statistical analysis shown in Figure 6f.

claim: Application of TFLLR in the presence of the glutamate receptor blockers, AP5/NBQX, failed to invoke statistically significant increases in either inward currents (pre-TFFLR: 89 ± 46 events/m, post-TFFLR: 96 ± 61 events/m, p=0.61, n = 15) or outward currents (pre-TFFLR: 40 ± 25 events/m, post-TFFLR: 52 ± 39 events/m, p=0.124, n = 15).
source: By contrast, the application of TFLLR in the presence of the glutamate receptor blockers, AP5/NBQX, failed to invoke statistically significant increases in either inward currents (pre-TFFLR: 89 ± 46 events/m, post-TFFLR: 96 ± 61 events/m, p=0.61, n = 15) or outward currents (pre-TFFLR: 40 ± 25 events/m, post-TFFLR: 52 ± 39 events/m, p=0.124, n = 15) (Figure 6g).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data with statistical analysis shown in Figure 6g.

claim: Astrocyte-mediated modulation of neuronal signaling occurs either through direct release of glutamate or release of a substance that acts directly on a glutamatergic neuron.
source: This result raises the possibility that astrocyte-mediated modulation of neuronal signaling occurs either through direct release of glutamate or release of a substance that acts directly on a glutamatergic neuron.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the experimental results showing that glutamate receptor blockade prevents both inward and outward current increases.

claim: TTX treatment prevented the post-stimulus increase in synaptic event frequency indicating that the events reflected the partial activation of the neuronal circuitry rather than direct astrocytic release.
source: This treatment prevented the post-stimulus increase in synaptic event frequency indicating that the events reflected the partial activation of the neuronal circuitry rather than direct astrocytic release.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing that TTX blocks the astrocyte-mediated increase in neuronal synaptic events.

claim: In MeCP2 globally null mice, astrocyte-mediated synaptic modulation is absent.
source: We further determine that in global MeCP2 null mice, this astrocyte-mediated synaptic modulation is absent and calcium signals in astrocytes are severely blunted.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing no increase in synaptic event frequency following astrocyte stimulation in MeCP2 null mice.

claim: Calcium signals in astrocytes are severely blunted in global MeCP2 null mice.
source: We further determine that in global MeCP2 null mice, this astrocyte-mediated synaptic modulation is absent and calcium signals in astrocytes are severely blunted.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental calcium imaging data showing reduced calcium responses in MeCP2 null astrocytes.

claim: Depolarization of MeCP2 null astrocytes showed no significant increase in astrocyte-mediated synaptic current frequency (pre-stim: 260 ± 140 events/m; post-stim: 267 ± 162 events/m; p=0.57; n = 10).
source: The absence of astrocyte-mediated effects was reflected in all MeCP2-deficient pairs tested (pre-stim: 260 ± 140 events/m; post-stim: 267 ± 162 events/m; p=0.57; n = 10; Figure 8c) (1.01 ± 0.04 fold; Figure 8d).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data with statistical analysis shown in Figures 8c-d.

claim: TFLLR application to MeCP2 null astrocytes showed no significant increase in event frequency (pre-TFLLR: 262 ± 131 events/m, post-TFLLR: 256 ± 111 events/m, p=0.68, n = 12).
source: Additionally, the cumulative data for all astrocyte-neuron pairs showed no significant increase in event frequency following agonist application (pre-TFLLR: 262 ± 131 events/m, post-TFLLR: 256 ± 111 events/m, p=0.68, n = 12) (Figure 8i).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data with statistical analysis shown in Figure 8i.

claim: Western blot analysis shows equivalent Par1 protein levels in MeCP2 null and wild-type mice.
source: even though immuno-labeling confirms astrocyte-specific Par1 expression in MeCP2 null cortex (Figure 3b) and Western blot analysis shows equivalent Par1 protein levels in MeCP2 null and wild-type mice (Figure 8—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental Western blot data shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 1.

claim: Depolarization of a MeCP2-positive astrocyte increased the frequency of neuronal synaptic events by 1.60 ± 0.23 fold (pre-stim: 150 ± 38 events/m, post-stim: 233 ± 77 events/m, p=0.04, n = 6) in mosaic mice.
source: Depolarization of the MeCP2 positive astrocyte increased the frequency of neuronal synaptic events by 1.60 ± 0.23 fold (pre-stim: 150 ± 38 events/m, post-stim: 233 ± 77 events/m, p=0.04, n = 6) (Figure 9b–c), recapitulating the findings from wild-type mice.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data with statistical analysis shown in Figures 9b-c.

claim: When MeCP2-negative astrocyte/neuronal pairs were tested, the frequency of neuronal synaptic currents did not increase (pre-stim: 147 ± 42 events/m, post-stim: 155 ± 38 events/m, p=0.24, n = 7).
source: When MeCP2-negative astrocyte/neuronal pairs were tested (Figure 9d), the frequency of neuronal synaptic currents did not increase (pre-stim: 147 ± 42 events/m, post-stim: 155 ± 38 events/m, p=0.24, n = 7) (Figure 9e–f) similar to the MeCP2 null males.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data with statistical analysis shown in Figures 9e-f.

claim: Depolarization of a MeCP2-positive astrocyte increased the frequency of synaptic currents in a neighboring MeCP2-negative neuron by 1.66 ± 0.25 fold (pre-stim: 189 ± 02 events/m, post-stim: 268 ± 96 events/m, p=0.02, n = 8).
source: depolarization of a MeCP2-positive astrocyte increased the frequency of synaptic currents in a neighboring MeCP2-negative neuron by 1.66 ± 0.25 fold (pre-stim: 189 ± 02 events/m, post-stim: 268 ± 96 events/m, p=0.02, n = 8) (Figure 9h–i).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data with statistical analysis shown in Figures 9h-i.

claim: When a MeCP2-negative astrocyte was paired with a MeCP2-positive neuron, depolarization failed to increase the frequency of synaptic currents (pre-stim: 176 ± 81 events/m, post-stim: 188 ± 83 events/m, p=0.1176, n = 10).
source: However, when a MeCP2-negative astrocyte was paired with a MeCP2-positive neuron (Figure 9j), depolarization failed to increase the frequency of synaptic currents (pre-stim: 176 ± 81 events/m, post-stim: 188 ± 83 events/m, p=0.1176, n = 10) (Figure 9k–l).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data with statistical analysis shown in Figures 9k-l.

claim: The astrocyte, not the neuron, requires MeCP2 expression in order to have a significant effect on astrocyte-mediated signaling within the local circuit.
source: Taken together, these experiments indicate that the astrocyte, not the neuron, requires MeCP2 expression in order to have a significant effect on astrocyte-mediated signaling within the local circuit.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the experimental data showing that MeCP2-positive astrocytes can activate MeCP2-negative neurons, but MeCP2-negative astrocytes cannot activate MeCP2-positive neurons.

claim: Dialysis with either BAPTA-based buffer reduced the basal frequency of neuronal events from the collective pre-stimulus levels by 0.72 ± 0.08 fold, along with no further increase in frequency following TFFLR application (p=0.02, n = 10).
source: Dialysis with either BAPTA-based buffer reduced the basal frequency of neuronal events from the collective pre-stimulus levels by 0.72 ± 0.08 fold, along with no further increase in frequency following TFFLR application (p=0.02, n = 10) (Figure 10a–b).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data with statistical analysis shown in Figures 10a-b.

claim: Increased intracellular calcium levels in astrocytes are required to support the astrocyte/neuronal signaling.
source: This demonstrates a requirement for increased intracellular calcium levels in astrocytes to support the astrocyte/neuronal signaling.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the experimental data showing that calcium buffering in astrocytes prevents the increase in neuronal synaptic activity.

claim: In all 23 wild-type astrocytes tested, somatic increases in calcium were observed in response to TFLLR application.
source: In all 23 wild-type astrocytes tested, somatic increases in calcium were observed in response to TFLLR application (Figure 10c).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental calcium imaging data shown in Figure 10c.

claim: Wild-type astrocytes produced rises in somatic calcium signals within one second of TFLLR application that required several seconds for complete relaxation to resting values.
source: Wild-type astrocytes produced rises in somatic calcium signals within one second of TFLLR application that required several seconds for complete relaxation to resting values (Figure 10d–e).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental calcium imaging data shown in Figures 10d-e.

claim: The overall mean for individual wild-type experiments corresponded to a ΔF/F0 of 0.60 ± 0.56 (n = 23).
source: The overall mean for individual experiments corresponded to a ΔF/F0 of 0.60 ± 0.56 (Figure 10f; n = 23).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental calcium imaging data shown in Figure 10f.

claim: 23 out of 34 tests of MeCP2 deficient astrocytes produced detectable calcium signals in response to TFLLR application.
source: Using the global MeCP2 null mice, 23 out of 34 tests of MeCP2 deficient astrocytes produced detectable calcium signals in response to TFLLR application (Figure 10d–f).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental calcium imaging data shown in Figures 10d-f.

claim: In MeCP2 deficient astrocytes that responded, the calcium signals followed a time course similar to wild-type but were significantly lower in intensity (mean ΔF/F0 = 0.27 ± 0.23; n = 23) (p=0.012).
source: In those 23 cases where responses were detected, the calcium signals followed a time course similar to wild-type (Figure 10d–e) but were significantly lower in intensity (mean ΔF/F0 = 0.27 ± 0.23; n = 23) (p=0.012) (Figure 10d–f).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental calcium imaging data with statistical analysis shown in Figures 10d-f.

claim: Photolysis in astrocytes effectively increased the somatic calcium levels for both wild-type (ΔF/F0 = 0.18 ± 0.06, n = 6) and MeCP2 null animals (ΔF/F0 = 0.26 ± 0.05, n = 4).
source: Photolysis in astrocytes effectively increased the somatic calcium levels for both wild-type (ΔF/F0 = 0.18 ± 0.06, n = 6) and MeCP2 null animals (ΔF/F0 = 0.26 ± 0.05, n = 4) (Figure 11—figure supplement 1a–c)
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental calcium imaging data shown in Figure 11—figure supplement 1a–c.

claim: In wild-type slices, uncaging of calcium loaded DMNP-EDTA resulted in an average 1.39 ± 0.08 fold increase in the frequency of synaptic currents in the neighboring neuron (pre-flash: 250 ± 94 events/m, post-flash: 326 ± 75 events/m, p=0.0003, n = 16).
source: In wild-type slices, uncaging of calcium loaded DMNP-EDTA resulted in an average 1.39 ± 0.08 fold increase in the frequency of synaptic currents in the neighboring neuron (pre-flash: 250 ± 94 events/m, post-flash: 326 ± 75 events/m, p=0.0003, n = 16) (Figure 11b,c).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data with statistical analysis shown in Figures 11b-c.

claim: Photolysis of wild-type astrocytes dialyzed with an empty cage did not alter the frequency of synaptic currents (pre-flash: 109 ± 66 events/m, post-flash: 115 ± 75 events/m, n = 4).
source: In control experiments, photolysis of wild-type astrocytes dialyzed with an empty cage did not alter the frequency of synaptic currents (pre-flash: 109 ± 66 events/m, post-flash: 115 ± 75 events/m, n = 4) (Figure 11—figure supplement 1d–f).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental control data shown in Figure 11—figure supplement 1d–f.

claim: When uncaging was repeated using MeCP2 null slices, there was no significant change in the frequency of synaptic currents (pre-flash: 227 ± 112 events/m, post-flash: 237 ± 121 events/m, p=0.23, n = 16).
source: When uncaging was repeated using MeCP2 null slices, one of the 16 pairs tested responded a large increase in event frequency. However, overall, there was no significant change in the frequency of synaptic currents (pre-flash: 227 ± 112 events/m, post-flash: 237 ± 121 events/m, p=0.23, n = 16) (Figure 11d–f).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data with statistical analysis shown in Figures 11d-f.

claim: The mechanisms in calcium handling that are associated with MeCP2 deficiency in astrocytes are not solely responsible for the reduced astrocyte-mediated stimulation of neurons.
source: From this result we surmise that the mechanisms in calcium handling that are associated with MeCP2 deficiency in astrocytes are not solely responsible for the reduced astrocyte-mediated stimulation of neurons.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the experimental result that calcium uncaging in MeCP2 null astrocytes failed to rescue the defective signaling.

claim: The most commonly reported form of astrocyte-mediated modulation of neuronal signaling involves changes in the frequency of neuronal synaptic currents mediated by the neurotransmitters GABA and glutamate.
source: The most commonly reported form of astrocyte-mediated modulation of neuronal signaling, also reflected in our study, involves changes in the frequency of neuronal synaptic currents mediated by the neurotransmitters GABA and glutamate (Kang et al., 1998; Benedetti et al., 2011; Araque et al., 1998; Fiacco and McCarthy, 2004; Jourdain et al., 2007; Liu et al., 2004).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to multiple studies: Kang et al., 1998; Benedetti et al., 2011; Araque et al., 1998; Fiacco and McCarthy, 2004; Jourdain et al., 2007; Liu et al., 2004.

claim: The increase in frequency for both neurotransmitters was not accompanied by increases in the average amplitudes, pointing to specific effects on presynaptic release and not postsynaptic receptors.
source: The increase in frequency for both neurotransmitters was not accompanied by increases in the average amplitudes, pointing to specific effects on presynaptic release and not postsynaptic receptors.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the experimental data showing frequency changes without amplitude changes.

claim: In p10-12 postnatal recordings from layers 2/3 cortical neurons in wild-type mice, GABA is excitatory.
source: In our p10-12 postnatal recordings from layers 2/3 cortical neurons in wild-type mice, GABA is excitatory, consistent with previous studies performed at this age (Ben-Ari, 2002).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data and a citation to Ben-Ari, 2002.

claim: Par1 receptor expresses at high levels in astrocytes.
source: The Par1 receptor expresses at high levels in astrocytes (Hermann et al., 2009; Park et al., 2015; Lee et al., 2007), a finding confirmed by our immunohistochemistry on cortical astrocytes.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Hermann et al., 2009; Park et al., 2015; Lee et al., 2007, and by experimental immunohistochemistry data.

claim: A small fraction of dentate gyrus neurons responded to TFLLR with a depolarizing response, and only under conditions where bath application was very long (>120 s).
source: In the best studied example, a small fraction of dentate gyrus neurons responded to TFLLR with a depolarizing response, and only under conditions where bath application was very long (>120 s) compared to our study (Han et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Han et al., 2011.

claim: Par1 in astrocytes stimulates adjacent neurons in the nucleus of the solitary tract.
source: Finally, our findings in cortex, that Par1 in astrocytes stimulates adjacent neurons, are supported by a previous study in the nucleus of the solitary tract (Vance et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Vance et al., 2015.

claim: The progression of overt RTT-like behaviors in mice is blunted following postnatal restoration of MeCP2 just in astrocytes.
source: For example, the progression of overt RTT-like behaviors in mice is blunted following postnatal restoration of MeCP2 just in astrocytes (Lioy et al., 2011), consistent with reversibility of the disease with ubiquitous MeCP2 expression (Guy et al., 2007).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Lioy et al., 2011.

claim: The disease is reversible with ubiquitous MeCP2 expression.
source: For example, the progression of overt RTT-like behaviors in mice is blunted following postnatal restoration of MeCP2 just in astrocytes (Lioy et al., 2011), consistent with reversibility of the disease with ubiquitous MeCP2 expression (Guy et al., 2007).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Guy et al., 2007.

claim: Astrocytes in a RTT mouse have reduced sensitivity in their detection of carbon dioxide in CNS respiratory centers.
source: Additionally, the astrocytes in a RTT mouse have reduced sensitivity in their detection of carbon dioxide in CNS respiratory centers (Turovsky et al., 2015) and the astrocytic expression of MeCP2 is critical in maintaining adaptive responses to respiratory CO2 chemosensitivity (Garg et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Turovsky et al., 2015.

claim: The astrocytic expression of MeCP2 is critical in maintaining adaptive responses to respiratory CO2 chemosensitivity.
source: Additionally, the astrocytes in a RTT mouse have reduced sensitivity in their detection of carbon dioxide in CNS respiratory centers (Turovsky et al., 2015) and the astrocytic expression of MeCP2 is critical in maintaining adaptive responses to respiratory CO2 chemosensitivity (Garg et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Garg et al., 2015.

claim: In the female RTT brain, only in the case where there is a wild-type astrocyte coupled to a neuron, will there be normal astrocyte-neuronal physiology.
source: This indicates that in the female RTT brain, only in the case where there is a wild-type astrocyte coupled to a neuron, will there be normal astrocyte-neuronal physiology.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the experimental data showing that MeCP2 expression in astrocytes is required for normal astrocyte-neuronal signaling.

claim: Calcium signaling pathways are often involved in gliotransmitter release.
source: What defects imparted by MeCP2 deficiency in astrocytes account for blunted neuronal signaling? Calcium signaling pathways are often involved in gliotransmitter release (Bazargani and Attwell, 2016) and both our ability to inhibit neuronal signaling through inclusion of a strong calcium buffer in the astrocyte as well as activation through calcium uncaging point to involvement of calcium (Kang et al., 1998; Benedetti et al., 2011; Bal-Price et al., 2002; Lee et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Bazargani and Attwell, 2016.

claim: TFFLR acts through the Par1 receptor to release calcium from intracellular stores.
source: Also, TFFLR acts through the Par1 receptor to release calcium from intracellular stores (Junge et al., 2004; Hollenberg et al., 1997; Ubl and Reiser, 1997).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Junge et al., 2004; Hollenberg et al., 1997; Ubl and Reiser, 1997.

claim: Both T type and L type voltage dependent calcium channels have been identified in acutely dissociated astrocytes.
source: Both T type and L type voltage dependent calcium channels have been identified in acutely dissociated astrocytes (Latour et al., 2003; Verkhratsky et al., 1998).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Latour et al., 2003; Verkhratsky et al., 1998.

claim: Loss of MeCP2 results in global gene expression changes in the brain, some of which have been linked to astrocytic functions that could impact signal transduction, such as microtubule dynamics and vesicle trafficking.
source: Given that loss of MeCP2 results in global gene expression changes in the brain, some of which have been linked to astrocytic functions that could impact signal transduction, such as microtubule dynamics and vesicle trafficking (Delépine et al., 2016), this result is not completely unexpected and underscores the complexity of alterations with the loss of MeCP2.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Delépine et al., 2016.

claim: There is a compromised ability of RTT mouse models to perform normal behavioral tasks.
source: The decreased signaling can account, at least in part, for the compromised ability of RTT mouse models to perform normal behavioral tasks, as well as for amelioration of RTT-like phenotypes after restoration of MeCP2 in astrocytes.
evidence: This claim draws from established knowledge about RTT mouse models.

claim: There is amelioration of RTT-like phenotypes after restoration of MeCP2 in astrocytes.
source: The decreased signaling can account, at least in part, for the compromised ability of RTT mouse models to perform normal behavioral tasks, as well as for amelioration of RTT-like phenotypes after restoration of MeCP2 in astrocytes.
evidence: This claim is supported by previous studies cited earlier in the manuscript.

claim: There is an altered excitatory-inhibitory (E/I) synaptic balance reported in RTT.
source: In addition to reduced overall excitatory neuronal signaling, there are potential implications reflected in an altered excitatory-inhibitory (E/I) synaptic balance reported in RTT (Feldman et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Feldman et al., 2016.

claim: The GABAAR switch from excitatory to inhibitory results from the expression of the chloride exporter KCC2, which establishes the asymmetrical trans-membrane concentration gradient.

claim: In both humans with RTT and mouse models, a delay in the expression of the chloride exporter occurs, thus causing developmental delay in the switch to inhibition.

evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Duarte et al., 2013; Tang et al., 2016; Feldman et al., 2016.

claim: The absence of astrocytic contributions to neuronal signaling in RTT places regions of the brain, which are critically dependent on E/I balance, at greater risk.

claim: Neurons and astrocytes could be distinguished by input resistance, which is four fold higher for neurons (143 ± 24 MΩ) compared to astrocytes (35 ± 12 MΩ).
source: Once the whole cell voltage clamp mode was established, cellular identity was confirmed on the basis of input resistance, which is four fold higher for neurons (143 ± 24 MΩ) compared to astrocytes (35 ± 12 MΩ).
evidence: This is a description of the experimental methods and measurements used in the study.
